introduction-the-128-bit-expansion.core: IPv4's 32 bits give about 4.3 billion addresses, long exhausted and patched with NAT. IPv6's 128 bits give 3.4×10³⁸, enough for every device to have globally unique addresses and every LAN a /64 subnet. It also simplifies headers, has no broadcast (multicast instead), and builds in autoconfiguration. The hard part is running both protocols during the long transition.

first_principles.problem: A mobile network can't get more IPv4 and relies on layers of NAT that break apps.

analogy.title: Switching from 7-digit to 20-digit phone numbers
analogy.story: Suddenly every device can have its own direct line instead of sharing a switchboard.
analogy.breaks: Phone number changes are coordinated; IPv6 adoption is gradual and uneven.

check.q: Why is a /64 the standard IPv6 LAN size?
check.a: SLAAC and neighbour discovery assume a 64-bit interface identifier, so /64 is required for autoconfiguration.

neighbor-discovery-protocol-ndp.core: NDP (over ICMPv6) replaces ARP and adds more. Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement resolve IPv6 addresses to MACs, using solicited-node multicast instead of broadcast. Router Solicitation and Advertisement let hosts find routers and prefixes. Duplicate Address Detection checks uniqueness, and redirects optimise paths. Because NDP is ICMPv6, filtering ICMPv6 breaks IPv6 entirely.

first_principles.problem: A firewall blocking ICMPv6 'for security' leaves IPv6 hosts unable to find their router.
truths: IPv6 has no ARP or broadcast.
derivation: Protect with **RA Guard** and SEND/ND inspection.

analogy.title: A neighbourhood intercom
analogy.story: Instead of shouting to the whole street, you buzz the small group whose house numbers end in the same digits.
analogy.breaks: Intercoms identify callers; NDP messages can be forged.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows router and neighbour discovery working.

code.text:
ip -6 neigh show
# fe80::1 dev eth0 lladdr 00:11:22:33:44:55 router REACHABLE
rdisc6 eth0     # solicit router advertisements

check.q: Why does blocking ICMPv6 break IPv6 networks?
check.a: Neighbour and router discovery (NDP) run over ICMPv6, so hosts can't resolve neighbours or find routers.

slaac-stateless-address-autoconfiguratio.core: With SLAAC a host configures itself without a server. It hears a Router Advertisement containing the /64 prefix, generates a 64-bit interface identifier, runs Duplicate Address Detection, and starts using the address. Privacy extensions (RFC 4941) and stable-privacy IDs (RFC 7217) replace the old MAC-derived EUI-64 identifiers so devices aren't trackable across networks. DNS servers can come via the RA's RDNSS option.

first_principles.problem: An IoT network has no DHCP server, yet hundreds of devices need working addresses.
derivation: Get DNS via **RDNSS** or stateless DHCPv6.

analogy.title: Choosing your own house number on a named street
analogy.story: The council tells you the street name; you pick a number nobody else uses and confirm by asking around.
analogy.breaks: House numbers are permanent; privacy addresses rotate.

code.text:
ip -6 addr show dev eth0
# inet6 2001:db8:1:2:3c4f:9a1e:77b2:10d4/64 scope global temporary dynamic
# inet6 2001:db8:1:2:a8f1:22ff:fe33:4455/64 scope global dynamic mngtmpaddr
# inet6 fe80::a8f1:22ff:fe33:4455/64 scope link

check.q: What problem do IPv6 privacy extensions solve?
check.a: MAC-derived EUI-64 addresses let devices be tracked across networks; temporary random IDs prevent that.

dhcpv6-stateful-control.core: DHCPv6 gives centralised control when SLAAC isn't enough: the server assigns specific addresses and keeps leases for audit and IPAM, plus options such as DNS and NTP. RA flags tell hosts what to do: the M (managed) flag means get addresses via DHCPv6, and the O (other) flag means get only options. DHCPv6 doesn't provide a default gateway (that always comes from RAs), and Android doesn't support stateful DHCPv6.

first_principles.problem: An enterprise must log which device had which IPv6 address for compliance, which SLAAC can't provide.
truths: Gateway info comes from RAs only.

analogy.title: Hotel-assigned rooms vs choosing your own
analogy.story: Reception assigns and records your room (DHCPv6); the corridor sign still shows the exit (RA).
analogy.breaks: Hotels identify guests by name; DHCPv6 uses DUIDs, not MACs.

check.q: Where does an IPv6 host get its default gateway when using DHCPv6?
check.a: Always from Router Advertisements; DHCPv6 doesn't provide a default route.

happy-eyeballs-the-dual-stack-race.core: On dual-stack hosts, a broken IPv6 path could make every connection wait for a timeout before trying IPv4. Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) races them. The client starts IPv6 first, and if it hasn't connected within about 250 ms it starts IPv4 in parallel, using whichever connects first and caching the result. That makes IPv6 deployment safe even when some paths are broken.

first_principles.problem: Users on a network with broken IPv6 routing see 20-second page loads waiting on IPv6 timeouts.

analogy.title: Calling someone's mobile and landline
analogy.story: Ring the mobile first, and if it doesn't pick up quickly, ring the landline too; talk on whichever answers.
analogy.breaks: Phone calls can't overlap politely; sockets can and the loser is closed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: IPv4 won because IPv6 was slow; user barely noticed.

code.text:
curl -v --happy-eyeballs-timeout-ms 250 https://example.com 2>&1 | grep -E 'Trying|Connected'
# Trying [2606:2800::1]:443...
# Trying 93.184.215.14:443...
# Connected to example.com (93.184.215.14)

check.q: What's a downside of Happy Eyeballs?
check.a: It masks broken IPv6, so operators may not notice problems unless they monitor IPv6 separately.

ipv6-only-vpcs-and-nat64dns64.core: Dual-stack doubles everything you configure and secure. IPv6-only subnets are simpler, but must still reach IPv4-only services. DNS64 synthesises AAAA records for IPv4-only names using the 64:ff9b::/96 prefix, and NAT64 translates those IPv6 packets to IPv4 at a gateway. AWS supports IPv6-only subnets with DNS64 on the resolver and NAT64 on NAT gateways.

first_principles.problem: A Kubernetes cluster exhausts private IPv4 space, but some dependencies are IPv4-only SaaS APIs.

analogy.title: A translator at the border
analogy.story: Travellers speaking only the new language reach old-language towns because a translator rewrites their requests.
analogy.breaks: Translators handle slang; NAT64 breaks apps with hardcoded IPv4 literals.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Pods reach IPv4 APIs via NAT64; no IPv4 needed in subnet.

check.a: For names with only A records, it synthesises AAAA records by embedding the IPv4 address in the NAT64 prefix (64:ff9b::/96).

ipv6-security-considerations.core: IPv6 isn't more or less secure, just different. Hosts often have global addresses with no NAT hiding them, so stateful firewalls must deny unsolicited inbound by default. Rogue RAs can hijack traffic, so use RA Guard. Extension headers can evade inspection, and tools and monitoring are often IPv4-only. Many networks have 'shadow IPv6' enabled by default on hosts without matching security policy.

first_principles.problem: A server hardened with IPv4 iptables rules is wide open over IPv6 because no ip6tables rules exist.

analogy.title: A building with a new side door nobody guards
analogy.story: The front door has a guard and locks, but the newly installed side door was left open.
analogy.breaks: Doors are visible; IPv6 exposure is invisible until scanned.

branches.label: Note
children: Large space hinders scanning, not a defence

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One ruleset covers IPv4 and IPv6 (inet family).

check.q: Why is NAT not a security control in IPv6 networks?
check.a: IPv6 hosts typically use global addresses without NAT, so a stateful firewall with default-deny inbound must provide the protection.
